content:
I've spent two weeks with ChatGPT and I want to set down what I think while the thinking is still fresh, three weeks after release, before the takes calcify and everyone sorts themselves into the positions they'll hold for the next five years.

This isn't a chatbot. I need to say that plainly, because the word chatbot is going to be used and it carries associations - Clippy, customer service bots, the systems that ask you to press 1 for English - that will cause a lot of intelligent people to misjudge what they're looking at.

What I'm looking at is a system that reads, writes, analyses, summarises, codes, translates, reasons through problems, explains concepts and generates coherent text on virtually any subject, at a level ranging from competent to occasionally remarkable. It makes mistakes. It hallucinates - producing confident, detailed, entirely fabricated information with no signal whatsoever that it's fabricating. It carries the blind spots and biases of its training data. In the precise technical sense it's a next-token prediction machine that doesn't understand, doesn't think and doesn't know anything at all.

And yet. I asked it to draft a contract clause and my lawyer friends called the result serviceable. I asked it to explain a difficult technical concept and got something clearer than most textbooks manage. I asked it to write code for a specific task and it worked first time. I asked it to analyse a business problem and got back the work a junior consultant produces after a week, in about thirty seconds. We've built something that can do a meaningful fraction of professional cognition without having any idea what it's doing. That's a genuinely strange thing to be alive for.

Most of the commentary this month has gone straight to the failures, and the people listing them are correct on every specific point. I don't think it matters much. A tool that's unreliable and instant and free beats a tool that's reliable and slow and expensive across an enormous range of real tasks, and the range widens with every model release. I've worked in product long enough to know the question is never what a system does on the day you meet it. The question is what the trajectory implies, and this trajectory needs no optimism to be alarming - only a straight line through the points we already have.

The observation I keep returning to is the one I find hardest to put down. The tasks this system does best are precisely the tasks we've spent thirty years telling young people to train for.

Research. Summarisation. Drafting. Analysis. The cognitive entry-level work that forms the base of every professional pyramid - what junior lawyers do, what junior accountants do, what graduate analysts and associate researchers and entry-level developers do. It's the work that justifies hiring someone with no experience, and it's the training ground where novices slowly turn into people who know things.

That work, at that level, is what the system does. Imperfectly and almost free, and the gap between imperfect and almost free is where the economics live. If a firm can buy eighty percent of junior-quality output for one percent of junior-quality cost, nobody needs a spreadsheet to work out what happens next.

The reassurance on offer is that every previous wave of automation created more work than it destroyed, and this one will too. I think that's probably right about the destination and dangerously vague about the route. Earlier transitions removed tasks over decades, which gave education systems and labour markets time to respond. This one is arriving inside a single product cycle, and it's aimed squarely at the rung people climb to become senior. Removing a rung doesn't only displace whoever is standing on it. It quietly stops producing the experienced practitioners of 2040, and nobody notices for fifteen years because the loss has no constituency and no press release.

Nobody knows how fast this goes from here. The researchers I trust disagree with each other about capability timelines by a factor of five, and anyone quoting a confident date is selling something. But when the uncertainty runs that wide and the thing at stake is the entry point to most professional careers, the sensible posture isn't confidence in either direction - it's acting now on the parts we can already see.

The step I'd argue for is narrower than the debate currently allows for, and it starts with the universities. Every institution in the country is right now drafting policy to detect and prohibit this technology in student work. I understand the integrity concern completely and I think the policy is a mistake of real historical proportions. We are proposing to train a generation to work without the instrument their entire working life will be conducted with, and to do it in the four years when they're cheapest to teach.

The alternative is to move what we assess, which nobody should confuse with giving up on assessment. If a free tool produces the graduate essay, then the graduate essay has stopped measuring anything and we should stop pretending otherwise. What remains scarce is judgement, taste, the ability to specify a problem precisely enough to be worth solving, and the ability to tell competent output from confident nonsense. That last one is going to matter more than anything else on the list, because the characteristic failure mode here is fluent fabrication, and we have never taught verification as a discipline in its own right. We're about to need it as a basic literacy.

Alongside that, somebody has to pay for the first rung deliberately, because firms won't do it out of civic feeling and the arithmetic argues against it every quarter. Training subsidies, professional bodies requiring intake, or partnerships simply recognising that a firm with no pipeline is running a slow liquidation with good margins. I don't much mind which mechanism. I mind that there currently isn't one.

A discontinuity is a step change rather than a gradual improvement - a moment when a technology crosses a threshold that changes the category of thing it can do. The iPhone was one. Nobody who queued for the first one was buying a better phone. They were buying a different object that happened to make calls, and it took most of the industry three years to work that out.

This is one. I don't know precisely what comes next and I'm suspicious of anyone who claims to, three weeks in. But a hundred million people found this thing in two months, which is the fastest adoption of anything ever built, and they didn't do it because of hype. They did it because it's useful right now, in ways that matter, in a world that hasn't adjusted to it yet.

The world changed in November 2022 and most people haven't noticed. That gap - between when something becomes true and when it becomes obvious - is the only real advantage any of us gets, and it closes fast. What we do with it will decide whether this technology arrives as the largest expansion of individual capability in living memory or as a decade of quiet displacement. Both are available. Neither is written.
